claim: A robust 'positive-negative' spectrum of behavioral and demographic variates, recently associated to covariation in brain function, can be identified using only structural features.
source: Our analyses reveal that a robust 'positive-negative' spectrum of behavioral and demographic variates, recently associated to covariation in brain function, can already be identified using only structural features, highlighting the importance of careful integration of structural features in any analysis of inter-individual differences in functional connectivity and downstream associations with behavioral/demographic variates.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, supported by the analyses described in the manuscript.

claim: The first quantitative approach to relate skull measures to human behavior or cognitive abilities dates to the first half of the 19th century.
source: The first quantitative approach intended to deepen such understanding dates to the first half of the 19-th century when skull measures were related to human behavior or cognitive abilities (Simpson, 2005; Fodor, 1983).
evidence: This historical claim is supported by citations to Simpson (2005) and Fodor (1983).

claim: Technical, intellectual and clinical advances in the last two centuries allow accurate quantification of brain structure and function.
source: Technical, intellectual and clinical advances in the last two centuries allow us to now accurately quantify brain structure and function (Lerch et al., 2017; Huettel et al., 2004; Friston et al., 2002; Woolrich et al., 2004; Rorden et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Functional connectivity patterns can be used to identify individuals.
source: for example, functional connectivity patterns can be used to identify individuals (Finn et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Finn et al., 2015.

claim: Functional connectivity patterns can predict fluid intelligence.
source: predict fluid intelligence (Finn et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Finn et al., 2015.

claim: A mode of functional connectivity variation relates to lifestyle, happiness and well-being.
source: or describe a mode of functional connectivity variation that relates to lifestyle, happiness and well-being (Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2015.

claim: Different brain structural features should reflect relationships with long-term demographic variables.
source: Furthermore, given the long-term character of some demographic variables (e.g. overall happiness), we hypothesize that different brain structural features, such as regional variation in the density of gray matter or subject-dependent degree of cortical expansion, should also reflect these relationships.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: Behavioral variations can be explained by more general brain structure variations than isolated single feature variations.
source: We further hypothesize that behavioral variations can be explained by more general brain structure variations than isolated single feature variations (e.g. cortical thickness variations)
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: Linked ICA increases statistical power by evidence integration across different features.
source: Such analyses increase statistical power by evidence integration across different features (Wolfers et al., 2017; Doan et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wolfers et al., 2017 and Doan et al., 2017.

claim: Linked ICA has been shown to be powerful in identifying correlated patterns of structural and diffusion spatial variation that can be studied in relation to individual behavioral and demographic measures.
source: and have been shown to be powerful in identifying correlated patterns of structural and diffusion spatial variation that can then be studied in relation to individual behavioral and demographic measures (Doan et al., 2017; Douaud et al., 2014; Francx et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doan et al., 2017, Douaud et al., 2014, and Francx et al., 2016.

claim: The study considers brain and behavioral data from close to 500 healthy young adults.
source: Although similar analyses have been previously performed (Douaud et al., 2014), in this work we benefit from the unique characteristics of the data sample; we consider brain and behavioral data from close to 500 'healthy young adults' which reduces common pathology- and age-related variance and increases the power to detect associations due to normal cross-sectional variability.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample size and characteristics.

claim: Considering healthy young adults reduces common pathology- and age-related variance and increases the power to detect associations due to normal cross-sectional variability.
source: we consider brain and behavioral data from close to 500 'healthy young adults' which reduces common pathology- and age-related variance and increases the power to detect associations due to normal cross-sectional variability.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the study design rationale.

claim: Structural brain features are strongly associated with demographic and behavioral variates.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that structural brain features are strongly associated with demographic and behavioral variates.
evidence: This is stated as a result supported by the study's findings.

claim: The most relevant mode of inter-individual variations across brain structural measures maps onto recent findings obtained using functional MRI data from the same HCP cohort.
source: Interestingly, the most relevant mode of inter-individual variations across brain structural measures identified through the multi-modal data fusion approach maps on to recent findings obtained using functional MRI data from the same HCP cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The findings closely resemble the 'positive-negative' set of behavioral measures identified in Smith et al. (2015) on the basis of functional (co-)variations.
source: In particular, our findings closely resemble the 'positive-negative' set of behavioral measures identified in Smith et al. (2015) on the basis of functional (co-)variations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding comparing the current results to Smith et al., 2015.

claim: Inter-individual differences attributed to brain function need to be reconsidered taking into account variations in brain structure across the cohort.
source: Using post-hoc analysis of the functional and structural modes we show that inter-individual differences attributed to brain function need to be reconsidered taking into account variations in brain structure across the cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the post-hoc analysis.

claim: The multi-modal structural brain data analyses resulted in a total of 100 collections of component maps.
source: The multi-modal structural brain data analyses (Figure 1, operations A and B) resulted in a total of 100 collections of component maps, each of which can be represented by a collection of 7 spatial maps covering the gray-matter space (voxel-based morphometry feature (VBM)), diffusion skeleton space (Fractional Anisotropy (FA), Mean Diffusivity (MD) and Anisotropy Mode (MO) features), cortical vertex space (cortical thickness (CT) and pial area (PA) features) and a voxel-wise map of the Jacobian deformation (JD).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: A total of 155 significant brain-behavior correlations were identified after FDR correction.
source: Post-hoc linear correlation analyses of these subject contributions with behavioral measures identified, after FDR correction (Figure 1, operations C, D and E, FDR corrected q < 2.2 × 10-4), a total of 155 significant brain-behavior correlations, summarized by 30 components reflecting at least one significant relationship to behavior.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical results.

claim: 30 components reflect at least one significant relationship to behavior.
source: a total of 155 significant brain-behavior correlations, summarized by 30 components reflecting at least one significant relationship to behavior.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: Component number six shows strong associations across a broad set of behavioral domains (48 measures) and across all structural modalities.
source: Only a single component (number 6) shows strong associations across a broad set of behavioral domains (48 measures) and across all structural modalities (i.e. is not dominated by one of the structural data types in that no single modality contributes >50% to the total variance of the component).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 6.

claim: Component 6 has relative contributions of 22% for VBM, 6% JD, 15% FA, 23% MD, 20% MO, 7% CT and 4% PA.
source: The relative contributions from the different modalities are 22% for VBM, 6% JD, 15% FA, 23% MD, 20% MO, 7% CT and 4% PA (Appendix 1—figure 1), reflecting a dominance of gray matter densities and diffusion measures and a lower involvement of the purely morphometric and cortical measures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the quantitative contributions of different modalities.

claim: Component 6 reflects a dominance of gray matter densities and diffusion measures and a lower involvement of the purely morphometric and cortical measures.
source: The relative contributions from the different modalities are 22% for VBM, 6% JD, 15% FA, 23% MD, 20% MO, 7% CT and 4% PA (Appendix 1—figure 1), reflecting a dominance of gray matter densities and diffusion measures and a lower involvement of the purely morphometric and cortical measures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative contributions.

claim: Component number six relates to various behavioral scores including working memory, language function and general wellbeing (life satisfaction, social support).
source: We observe that component number six relates to various behavioral scores including working memory, language function and general wellbeing (life satisfaction, social support).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the behavioral associations found.

claim: VBM measures for component 6 are most heavily weighted in bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, temporal pole, lingual gyrus and the putamen.
source: In Figure 2 we present the associated spatial maps: VBM measures are most heavily weighted in bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, temporal pole, lingual gyrus and the putamen (first row).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Morphometric differences (JD features) for component 6 load into temporal lobes, caudate and brainstem.
source: Morphometric differences (JD features) load into temporal lobes, caudate and brainstem (second row)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: White matter tracts for component 6 most heavily weigh onto the internal capsule, anterior thalamic radiation and the anterior corona radiata.
source: and white matter tracts do most heavily weigh onto the internal capsule, anterior thalamic radiation and the anterior corona radiata (3rd, 4th, and 5th rows).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cortical effects for component 6 are largely associations with multi-modal association cortex while primary sensory cortices are not implicated.
source: Cortical effects (6th and 7th rows) are largely associations with multi-modal association cortex that show effects whereas primary sensory cortices are not implicated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The involvement of areas such as the putamen and lingual gyrus are relevant to explain the behavioral relationships found with working memory and word processing.
source: Note that the involvement of areas such as the putamen and lingual gyrus are relevant to explain the behavioral relationships found with working memory and word processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking brain regions to behavioral functions.

claim: The involvement of structural connections between subcortical and prefrontal areas as well as the orbitofrontal cortex and temporal poles could explain the link to more complex functions such as emotional support or life satisfaction.
source: Furthermore, the involvement of structural connections between subcortical and prefrontal areas as well as the orbitofrontal cortex and temporal poles could explain the link to more complex functions such as emotional support or life satisfaction.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking brain connectivity to behavioral functions.

claim: Component one relates mainly to gender, physical strength and language.
source: Component one relates mainly to gender, physical strength and language and it is defined by significant changes in gray matter density (VBM measures) and cortical areal expansion (PA measure).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the behavioral associations for component 1.

claim: Component one is defined by significant changes in gray matter density (VBM measures) and cortical areal expansion (PA measure).
source: Component one relates mainly to gender, physical strength and language and it is defined by significant changes in gray matter density (VBM measures) and cortical areal expansion (PA measure).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the modalities contributing to component 1.

claim: Component one's associated spatial patterns appear to reflect brain size and cortical area differences in both temporal lobes.
source: Its associated spatial patterns appear to in fact reflect brain size and cortical area differences in both temporal lobes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial patterns for component 1.

claim: Component two is driven by VBM maps and correlates with variations in gender, age, height, weight and strength.
source: Similarly, component two is driven by VBM maps and correlates with variations in gender, age, height, weight and strength.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 2.

claim: Component two's spatial extent includes the paracingulate gyrus and bilateral insular and opercular cortex.
source: Its spatial extent includes the paracingulate gyrus and bilateral insular and opercular cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the spatial extent for component 2.

claim: Components 7, 24, 25, 29 and 55 are driven by at least three feature modalities and they map into gender, weight, body mass and height.
source: Components 7, 24, 25, 29 and 55 are driven by at least three feature modalities and they map into gender, weight, body mass and height.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for these components.

claim: Component seven maps into gender and shows cingulate gyrus and insular cortex.
source: Component seven maps into gender and shows cingulate gyrus and insular cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 7.

claim: Component 24 maps into weight and body mass and is mapped into putamen, intracalcarine cortex and thalamus.
source: Component 24 maps into weight and body mass and is mapped into putamen, intracalcarine cortex and thalamus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 24.

claim: Components 25 and 29 relate height with the inferior temporal gyrus and the cerebellum together with strong DWI weightings in the brainstem.
source: Components 25 and 29 relate height with the inferior temporal gyrus and the cerebellum together with strong DWI weightings in the brainstem.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for components 25 and 29.

claim: Component 55 relates to weight and maps into the precentral gyrus and asymmetric differences in DWI measures.
source: Component 55 relates to weight and maps into the precentral gyrus and asymmetric differences in DWI measures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 55.

claim: Component 89 maps VBM and JD into hematocrit and involves the lingual and occipital fusiform gyrus.
source: Number 89 maps VBM and JD into hematocrit and involves the lingual and occipital fusiform gyrus.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 89.

claim: Component 20 maps JD and VBM in the posterior midline into age and relationship status.
source: Finally, component 20 maps JD and VBM in the posterior midline into age and relationship status.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the findings for component 20.

claim: Component number six is recovered at dimensionalities 90 and 110 with a subject mode correlation value of around r ~ 0.9.
source: In particular, component number six is recovered at dimensionalities 90 and 110 with a subject mode correlation value of around r ~ 0.9 (details can be found in Appendix 1, section 'Robustness: model order').
evidence: This is a direct statement of the robustness analysis results.

claim: Analysis excluding the JD revealed essentially unaltered brain-behavior associations.
source: Regarding the influence of purely morphometric differences in the analyses, a comparative analysis excluding the JD revealed essentially unaltered brain-behavior associations.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the robustness analysis results.

claim: Analysis of the JD feature in isolation showed that no fully corrected significant association to the reported positive-negative structural mode is found when considering uniquely morphometric differences.
source: Analysis of the JD feature in isolation showed that no fully corrected significant association to the reported positive-negative structural mode is found when considering uniquely morphometric differences, even if considering several components together.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: The structural mode (component 6) and the functional mode reported in Smith et al. (2015) are significantly correlated (r = 0.4643, r2 = 0.21, permutation p<10−5).
source: With the analysis restricted to the 421 subjects common to both studies, we found that the structural and the functional subject modes are significantly correlated (r = 0.4643, r2 = 0.21, permutation p<10−5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical comparison results.

claim: Post-hoc correlation analyses to behavior replicated the original functional positive-negative mode by identifying 60 functional-behavioral relationships.
source: Post-hoc correlation analyses to behavior replicated the original functional positive-negative mode by identifying 60 functional-behavioral relationships (Smith et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a direct statement of the replication analysis results.

claim: 22 of the behavioral measures associated with the functional mode are also associated to the structural mode.
source: we found that 22 of these behavioral measures are also associated to the structural mode and that there is no significant difference in the correlation values provided by the functional or the structural analyses at these intersecting behavioral measures
evidence: This is a direct statement of the overlap analysis results.

claim: There is no significant difference in the correlation values provided by the functional or the structural analyses at the intersecting behavioral measures.
source: we found that 22 of these behavioral measures are also associated to the structural mode and that there is no significant difference in the correlation values provided by the functional or the structural analyses at these intersecting behavioral measures
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical comparison results.

claim: The structural mode removes 73% of the 60 associations originally found using functional data.
source: The post-hoc correlation analysis of the residualised functional mode to behavior revealed a significant decrease in correlation (mean r decrease = 0.078, p<0.01) that result in the structural mode removing 73% of the 60 associations originally found using functional data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the residualization analysis results.

claim: The remaining 16 significant relationships after residualization involve measures as handedness, education, tobacco use, list sorting, delay discount, and intelligence.
source: The remaining 16 significant relationships involve measures as handedness, education, tobacco use, list sorting, delay discount, and intelligence.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the residualization analysis results.

claim: The structural-functional Linked-ICA analyses recovered the positive-negative mode reported in the originally reported multi-modal structural analyses.
source: This structural-functional analysis recovered the positive-negative mode reported in the originally reported multi-modal structural analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the combined analysis results.

claim: Component 16 from the structural-functional analysis significantly correlates (r = 0.89, p<10^−5) with the mainly reported structural mode (component 6).
source: More concretely, we found a component, number 16, significantly correlating (r = 0.89, p<10^−5) with the mainly reported structural mode (component 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The functional data marginally contributes (0.0012%) to the positive-negative mode in the structural-functional analysis.
source: The contribution of each modality to this mode equals 20% for VBM, 15.6% for FA, 24.4% for MD, 23.9% for MO, 7% for CT, 3% for PA, 5% for JD and 0.0012% for the functional partial correlation feature.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the modality contributions.

claim: Structure in its own can explain the positive-negative behavioral mode.
source: While all structural features reflect approximately the same contribution as in the original structural analyses, it is interesting that the functional data does marginally contribute to the found mode, suggesting that structure in its own can explain the positive-negative behavioral mode.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modality contribution results.

claim: Causal analysis estimated a likelihood ratio of ~0.04, indicating a significant structure to function causation effect (p<0.0025).
source: This analysis estimated a likelihood ratio of ~0.04, that is a significant structure to function causation effect (p<0.0025, using permutation testing) (Hyvarinen and Smith, 2013)
evidence: This is a direct statement of the causal analysis results.

claim: Replication causal analysis using HCP1200 sample estimated a likelihood ratio of ~0.09, indicating a significant structure-to-function causation effect (p<0.005).
source: Furthermore, consecutive causal analyses from the structural mode to the functional mode estimated a likelihood ratio of ~0.09, that is a significant structure-to-function causation effect (p<0.005).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the replication causal analysis results.

claim: The spatial organization of component 6 predominantly includes regions and connections that are relevant to working memory and word processing such as the putamen and lingual gyrus.
source: Accordingly, the spatial organization of the component that relates to these measures predominantly includes regions and connections that are relevant to working memory and word processing such as the putamen and lingual gyrus (Mechelli et al., 2000; Arsalidou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial patterns supported by citations.

claim: The putamen and lingual gyrus are relevant to working memory and word processing.
source: regions and connections that are relevant to working memory and word processing such as the putamen and lingual gyrus (Mechelli et al., 2000; Arsalidou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mechelli et al., 2000 and Arsalidou et al., 2013.

claim: The results relate to the ones presented in Finn et al. (2015) since it identifies fluid intelligence measures.
source: Furthermore, the mode of structural variation we report here relates to several recently reported results obtained using functional MRI. In particular, our results relate to the ones presented in Finn et al. (2015) since it identifies fluid intelligence measures
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior work.

claim: The structural mode and the functional mode are strongly correlated subject measures (r = 0.46).
source: in fact, the structural mode and the functional mode are strongly correlated subject measures (r = 0.46).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the correlation between modes.

claim: The analyses reliably augment the spectrum of behavioral variables reported by the functional analyses by extending it with many working memory, language, relational task, ASR and DSM measures.
source: Our analyses reliably augment the spectrum of behavioral variables reported by the functional analyses by extending it with many working memory, language, relational task, ASR and DSM measures (Figure 1 bottom right and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of how the current results extend prior findings.

claim: The functional mode of variation is strongly associated with connectivity in brain areas approximately resembling the Default Mode Network.
source: In fact, the functional mode of variation is strongly associated with connectivity in brain areas approximately resembling the Default Mode Network (Smith et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2015.

claim: White matter structure variations could contribute to the functional connectivity changes reported in Smith et al. (2015).
source: and, given the spatial extent and the strong weight of the DWI data in the structural mode we report, it seems reasonable to assume that these white matter structure variations could contribute to the functional connectivity changes reported in Smith et al. (2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking structural and functional findings.

claim: There is no clear spatial overlap between the reported structural mode and the cortical functional extent of the 'positive-negative' mode.
source: Further, we found no clear spatial overlap between the reported structural mode and the cortical functional extent of the 'positive-negative' mode
evidence: This is a direct statement of the spatial comparison results.

claim: Integrated functional-structural analyses should increase the sensitivity of both functional and structural analyses.
source: suggesting that integrated functional-structural analyses should increase the sensitivity of both functional and structural analyses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Group functional connectivity measures using fMRI may be biased due to individual structural differences that may become 'visible' in the analysis of functional cross-subject.
source: Further, these results might question whether group functional connectivity measures using fMRI provide direct measures of brain connectivity or are biased due to individual structural differences that may become 'visible' in the analysis of functional cross-subject.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation questioning the interpretation of functional connectivity measures.

claim: The structural features relating to the behavioral mode are not uniquely driven by morphometric differences.
source: These extra analyses confirm that the structural features relating to the behavioral mode are not uniquely driven by morphometric differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the robustness analyses.

claim: Many associations previously attributed to functional connectivity are already present at the structural level.
source: As such, our results confirm that many associations previously attributed to functional connectivity are already present at the structural level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of structural and functional results.

claim: Functional imaging shows specialization towards a specific subset of behavioral measures for which it provides strong effects even after linear accounting for the structural findings.
source: This could be interpreted in terms of a specialization of functional imaging towards a specific subset of behavioral measures for which it provides strong effects even after linear accounting for the structural findings
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residualization analysis results.

claim: Not all previously identified associations can be explained through inter-individual differences in brain structure.
source: implying that not all previously identified associations can be explained through inter-individual differences in brain structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the residualization analysis.

claim: The two modes (structural and functional) are significantly overlapping measures that are not fully reflected in the Jacobian deformation field.
source: As such, these two modes are significantly overlapping measures that are not fully reflected in the Jacobian deformation field.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analyses of structural and functional modes.

claim: The presence of residual functional associations to behavior suggests that these associations cannot uniquely be attributed to simple morphometric differences.
source: The presence of residual functional associations to behavior suggests that these associations - although possibly influenced by structural variation - cannot uniquely be attributed to simple morphometric differences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residualization analysis results.

claim: The results align with recent findings by Bijsterbosch et al. (2018) who show that individual spatial configurations extracted from functional MRI rather than the connectivity profiles between areas seem to stronger relate to the positive-negative mode.
source: These results align with recent findings by Bijsterbosch et al. (2018) who show that individual spatial configurations extracted from functional MRI rather than the connectivity profiles between areas seem to stronger relate to the positive-negative mode.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior work.

claim: The association between imaging phenotypes and behavioral/demographic measures may involve non-linear relationships that remain incompletely accounted for within linear analytical frameworks.
source: It is entire possible that the association between imaging phenotypes and behavioral/demographic measures involve non-linear relationships that remain at best incompletely accounted for within these analytical frameworks.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of the analytical approach.

claim: Residualised analysis where functional variations are regressed from the structural mode leaves only 7 out of 48 associations significant.
source: Indeed, in such a case only 7 out of 48 associations remain significant (relating to weight, antisocial behavior (DSM), family structure problems, relational task or adult self-report (ASR) questions, see Appendix 1, section 'On the power of structural and functional associations to behavior').
evidence: This is a direct statement of the reverse residualization analysis results.

claim: The results suggest a segregation of different structural and functional specializations towards different behavioral measures.
source: These results suggest a segregation of different structural and functional specializations towards different behavioral measures with for example, intelligence being, not only, but more related to brain function, and antisocial or relational task measures relating more strongly to brain structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bidirectional residualization results.

claim: Intelligence is more related to brain function.
source: with for example, intelligence being, not only, but more related to brain function
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residualization analysis results.

claim: Antisocial or relational task measures relate more strongly to brain structure.
source: and antisocial or relational task measures relating more strongly to brain structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residualization analysis results.

claim: The likelihood of the structural mode causally influencing the functional mode is >20 times higher than the likelihood of the reverse causation.
source: Finally, a causal analysis revealed a significant structural to functional mode causation (Hyvarinen and Smith, 2013) where the likelihood of the structural mode causally influencing the functional mode (from Smith et al., 2015) is >20 times higher than the likelihood of the reverse causation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the causal analysis results.

claim: Structural variations will enter as mediating factor in any functional analysis pipeline and need to be accounted for suitably.
source: Nevertheless, these causal findings align with the fact that cross-subject analysis of functional data typically necessitates processing of structural data (e.g. through co-registration into a common space). As such, structural variations will enter as mediating factor in any functional analysis pipeline and need to be accounted for suitably.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the causal findings in the context of fMRI processing pipelines.

claim: There is no reverse influence of functional variations in the analysis of structural measures.
source: However, there is no reverse influence of functional variations in the analysis of structural measures.
evidence: This is a statement about the asymmetry in the analysis pipelines.

claim: Future work will have to focus on robustifying functional MRI analysis with regard to cross-subject variations in brain structure.
source: Such dependencies remain poorly modeled in current analysis procedures and future work will have to focus on robustifying functional MRI analysis with regard to cross-subject variations in brain structure, for example by more advanced alignment procedures and/or through derivation of functional measures that are invariant under variations in structure.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings.

claim: The findings will have important implications for the interpretation of future finding across neuroimaging 'big data' studies.
source: This will have important implications for the interpretation of future finding across neuroimaging 'big data' studies and will help improve our understanding of the functional-structural integration and its relation to behavioral associations.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The study uses data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) N = 500 release.
source: In this work, we use data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) N = 500 release which contains data from healthy young adults including twins and their non-twin siblings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data source.

claim: The HCP N = 500 release contains data from healthy young adults including twins and their non-twin siblings.
source: In this work, we use data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) N = 500 release which contains data from healthy young adults including twins and their non-twin siblings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample characteristics.

claim: Each HCP subject participated in structural, diffusion and several functional MRI recordings.
source: In addition to performing more than 300 behavioral/demographic tests, each subject participated in structural, diffusion and several functional MRI recordings (Van Essen et al., 2012; Elam and Van Essen, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collected, supported by citations.

claim: From the initial N = 500 participants, several subjects were excluded on the basis of abnormalities in any of the features, resulting in N = 448 subjects entered into further analyses.
source: From the initial N = 500 participants, several subjects were excluded on the basis of abnormalities in any of the features. In total, N = 448 subjects were entered into further analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size after exclusions.

claim: Linked-ICA is an extension of Bayesian ICA to multiple input sets, where all individual ICA factorizations are linked through a shared common mixing matrix.
source: In brief, Linked-ICA is an extension of Bayesian ICA (Choudrey, 2002) to multiple input sets, where all individual ICA factorizations are linked through a shared common mixing matrix that reflect the subject-wise contribution to each component.
evidence: This is a description of the Linked-ICA method, supported by citation.

claim: The study reports full results from a 100 dimensional factorization.
source: Given our sample size and following (Groves et al., 2011; Groves et al., 2012) we report full results from a 100 dimensional factorization.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dimensionality choice, supported by citations.

claim: The study uses Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) to take into account the family structure present in the HCP sample while assessing significance.
source: To take into account the family structure present in the HCP sample while assessing significance we use the Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) (Winkler et al., 2014; Winkler et al., 2015) and use 106 permutations per tested correlation
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical method used, supported by citations.

claim: The study uses 10^6 permutations per tested correlation.
source: and use 106 permutations per tested correlation (Figure 1 operation D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of permutations used.

claim: Significance is defined at p<0.05 and multiple comparison is addressed by applying FDR correction as well as full Bonferroni correction.
source: We define significance at p<0.05 and address the multiple comparison by applying FDR correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) as well as full Bonferroni correction (Figure 1 operation E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical thresholds and corrections used.
